title: Episode 126: John Tyler and the Annexation of Texas: The Secret Treaty That Reshaped North America

In eighteen forty-three, the Republic of Texas stood at a perilous historical crossroads. Seven years after winning independence from Mexico at the Battle of San Jacinto, the young Lone Star Republic was financially bankrupt, sparsely populated, and lived under the constant threat of Mexican reconquest. Both Andrew Jackson and Martin Van Buren had rejected Texas's petitions for annexation, terrified that bringing a massive slaveholding territory into the Union would ignite civil war with Northern abolitionists.

Seeing America's hesitation, the British Empire moved aggressively to step into the vacuum. British diplomats offered Texas financial loans and military protection in exchange for Texas abolishing slavery and remaining an independent satellite republic—creating a British-dominated cotton rival on the southern flank of the United States that would block American westward expansion forever.

Facing total political isolation in Washington, President John Tyler recognized this existential threat. Working in utmost secrecy with Texas President Sam Houston, Tyler launched a clandestine diplomatic campaign to annex Texas. Even when a catastrophic cannon explosion aboard the warship USS Princeton killed his Secretary of State and nearly killed Tyler himself, the President refused to abandon the mission. Appointing John C. Calhoun to complete the pact, and executing an unprecedented constitutional maneuver through a joint resolution of Congress, Tyler signed the annexation of Texas just three days before leaving the White House. Here is George with the story of the treaty that reshaped a continent.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our exploration of President John Tyler with one of the boldest, most consequential geopolitical triumphs in American history: the Annexation of Texas. In the eighteen-forties, Texas was an independent republic facing economic ruin and Mexican invasion, while Great Britain plotted to turn it into an imperial satellite. Rejected by his own party and facing ferocious opposition in Congress, President Tyler launched a high-stakes campaign that added nearly four hundred thousand square miles to the United States. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE LONE STAR AT THE CROSSROADS
In eighteen forty-three, the Republic of Texas was a nation living on borrowed time. Seven years had passed since General Sam Houston's ragtag Texian army had shattered the legions of Mexican General Santa Anna at the Battle of San Jacinto, establishing the independent Lone Star Republic. But Mexico adamantly refused to recognize Texan independence, treating Texas as a rebellious province and launching recurring military cavalry raids that sacked San Antonio in eighteen forty-two.
Domestically, the young republic was on the brink of fiscal collapse. With a population of fewer than one hundred and fifty thousand citizens scattered across a territory larger than all of France, Texas was crushed under ten million dollars of national debt. Its paper currency, the 'redback,' had plummeted until it was worth barely two cents on the dollar, and the government lacked funds even to buy gunpowder for its militia.
From the moment of its independence, the vast majority of Texans had desperately desired annexation to the United States. They were culturally and spiritually Americans—former Tennessee frontiersmen, Virginia farmers, and Kentucky riflemen who had answered the call of Stephen F. Austin and Davy Crockett. In their very first popular referendum in eighteen thirty-six, the citizens of Texas had voted overwhelmingly, by more than ninety-nine percent, in favor of immediately joining the United States.
Yet in Washington, their impassioned pleas had been flatly and repeatedly rejected. Both Andrew Jackson and Martin Van Buren had slammed the door of the White House in their faces. Annexation was political dynamite that terrified Northern politicians: Northern anti-slavery Whigs, spearheaded by former President John Quincy Adams in the House of Representatives, declared that annexing Texas was an unholy, imperial conspiracy of Southern slaveholders designed to carve five or six new slave states out of the Southwest. Abolitionists warned that bringing Texas into the Union would violate treaties, trigger an immediate war with Mexico, and ignite a catastrophic civil war that would rip the United States apart. Humiliated, impoverished, and despairing of American brotherhood, Texas President Sam Houston began playing a dangerous, sophisticated game of international diplomacy, turning his gaze across the Atlantic toward the waiting arms of the British Empire.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SHADOW OF THE BRITISH EMPIRE
Great Britain, the world's reigning superpower, saw in Texas an incomparable geopolitical opportunity. British Foreign Secretary Lord Aberdeen recognized that an independent Texas could become the ultimate strategic counterweight to the rising power of the United States. Britain's textile mills in Manchester and Lancashire were dangerously dependent on Southern American cotton. If Britain could secure an exclusive free-trade alliance with Texas, British mills would have an independent cotton supply, breaking America's cotton monopoly.
Furthermore, British diplomats proposed a grand bargain: Great Britain would guarantee the independence of Texas against Mexican reconquest, pressure Mexico to formally recognize Texan borders, and provide millions in loans. In return, Texas would agree to abolish slavery, adopt complete free trade with British goods, and pledge never to unite with the United States. A British satellite in Texas would permanently encircle the United States from the south and west, blocking American expansion to the Pacific Ocean forever.
When intelligence of these British diplomatic maneuvers reached President John Tyler in the autumn of eighteen forty-three, he was galvanized into action. Tyler understood that Texas was the fulcrum of continental destiny. If Great Britain gained a foothold on the Gulf of Mexico, the United States would be trapped on the eastern half of the continent, facing a hostile British empire in Canada to the north and a British protectorate in Texas to the south. Tyler declared to his confidants: 'Texas must be ours, or she will be Britain's.'

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SECRET DIPLOMACY OF ABEL UPSHUR
Operating in total secrecy to avoid alerting Northern anti-slavery congressmen or British spies, Tyler tasked his brilliant new Secretary of State, Abel P. Upshur of Virginia, with opening confidential negotiations with Texan diplomats. In Washington, Upshur met in darkened drawing rooms with Texan minister Isaac Van Zandt. Upshur assured the Texans that Tyler was prepared to throw the full power of the United States behind immediate annexation, assuming Texas's national debt and deploying the United States Navy to the Gulf of Mexico to protect Texas from Mexican retaliation while the treaty was pending.
Sam Houston, playing a masterly game of diplomatic poker, played the United States and Great Britain against one another. Houston let it be known in Washington that British warships were anchored at Galveston and that British diplomats were offering protection, forcing Tyler and Upshur to move with feverish urgency.
By February eighteen forty-four, Upshur and Van Zandt had completed the secret treaty of annexation. The parchment lay on Upshur's desk, awaiting final signatures. Tyler planned to send the treaty to the Senate in triumph, accompanied by an appeal to national patriotism that would unite the country and secure his own re-election. But just as the triumph was within their grasp, an appalling catastrophe struck the administration.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: DISASTER ON THE USS PRINCETON
On February twenty-eighth, eighteen forty-four, President Tyler, his cabinet, and four hundred dignitaries—including senators, diplomats, and prominent Washington society ladies—boarded the state-of-the-art steam warship USS Princeton for a celebratory cruise down the Potomac River. The centerpiece of the ship was the 'Peacemaker'—the largest wrought-iron naval cannon in the world, capable of firing a two-hundred-and-twenty-five-pound cannonball five miles.
Throughout the sunny afternoon, the giant gun was fired several times to the delight of the crowd. As the ship approached Mount Vernon on the return voyage, Secretary of the Navy Thomas Gilmer requested one final salute in honor of George Washington. President Tyler was below deck in the ship's saloon, singing a humorous sea shanty with his future young bride, Julia Gardiner, when the gun was fired.
Tragedy struck with deafening horror. The breech of the massive cannon fractured under the explosive pressure, detonating like a gigantic bomb. Lethal chunks of jagged iron tore through the crowded deck. Secretary of State Abel Upshur, Secretary of the Navy Gilmer, and four others, including Julia Gardiner's father, were killed instantly. Dozens of sailors and guests were maimed by flying shrapnel. Tyler dashed on deck to find a scene of carnage, with his closest cabinet advisers lying dead in pools of blood. Had Tyler not paused below deck to listen to the song, he too would have been killed.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: CALHOUN AND THE DEFEAT IN THE SENATE
Despite his profound grief, John Tyler refused to let the catastrophe derail his grand continental strategy. To replace the fallen Upshur, Tyler made a fateful decision: he appointed former Vice President John C. Calhoun of South Carolina as Secretary of State. Calhoun was a legendary statesman whose name commanded immense respect across the South, and he finalized the treaty of annexation within two weeks.
However, Calhoun committed a disastrous political blunder. In transmitting the treaty to the Senate in April eighteen forty-four, Calhoun included an official diplomatic letter to the British minister, Richard Pakenham. In the 'Pakenham Letter,' Calhoun explicitly defended Texas annexation not as a national security measure, but as an essential defense of the institution of human slavery, arguing that slavery was a positive good that must be protected against British abolitionism.
Calhoun's letter ignited a firestorm of outrage across the North. Anti-slavery Whigs, who might have supported annexation for national security reasons, now saw the treaty as a brazen slaveholder conspiracy. Henry Clay and Martin Van Buren, both seeking the presidency in eighteen forty-four, issued public letters opposing immediate annexation. On June eighth, eighteen forty-four, the United States Senate decisively rejected Tyler's treaty by a crushing vote of thirty-five to sixteen. To all observers, Texas annexation was dead.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE JOINT RESOLUTION MASTERSTROKE
Most presidents would have admitted defeat, but John Tyler refused to surrender. In the presidential election of eighteen forty-four, Texas annexation became the central, explosive issue. The Democratic Party discarded Martin Van Buren and nominated dark-horse candidate James K. Polk of Tennessee, who campaigned on the bold, expansionist platform of the 'Re-annexation of Texas and Re-occupation of Oregon.' Polk defeated Henry Clay, sweeping to victory on a wave of westward expansionism that became known as 'Manifest Destiny.'
Tyler seized upon Polk's election as a decisive mandate from the American people. But Tyler faced a technical constitutional obstacle: a formal treaty required a two-thirds majority in the Senate, which annexation still lacked. Tyler executed an unprecedented constitutional maneuver: he proposed annexing Texas not by treaty, but by a Joint Resolution of Congress, which required only a simple majority vote in both the House and Senate.
Critics screamed that this was an unconstitutional evasion of the treaty clause, but Tyler pushed the measure forward with relentless energy. In late February eighteen forty-five, the Joint Resolution passed the House and squeezed through the Senate by a razor-thin vote of twenty-seven to twenty-five. On March first, eighteen forty-five—just three days before leaving office—President John Tyler signed the historic resolution offering immediate statehood to the Republic of Texas.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LONE STAR JOINS THE CONSTELLATION
Tyler's decisive act transformed the geopolitical map of the Western Hemisphere forever. Knowing that British diplomats in Texas were still frantically attempting to broker an eleventh-hour peace treaty between Mexico and Texas to block annexation, Tyler dispatched a fast courier carrying the signed joint resolution across the Gulf of Mexico. When the news reached Austin and Galveston, church bells pealed, twenty-eight-gun artillery salutes shook the plains, and citizens wept with joy in the streets. In July eighteen forty-five, a special constitutional convention in Texas voted overwhelmingly, with only one dissenting vote, to accept American statehood. On December twenty-ninth, eighteen forty-five, under President James K. Polk, Texas was formally admitted as the twenty-eighth state of the Union, and the Lone Star flag was lowered as the Stars and Stripes rose above the capitol in Austin.
The annexation of Texas added nearly three hundred and ninety thousand square miles of magnificent territory to the United States—an empire larger than France, Great Britain, and Germany combined. It secured the American frontier on the Rio Grande, slammed the door permanently on British imperial ambitions in the American Southwest, and set in motion the unstoppable continental chain of events that would carry American sovereignty to the shores of the Pacific Ocean in California.
John Tyler had entered the White House in eighteen forty-one as an accidental president, ridiculed as 'His Accidency,' abandoned by his cabinet, and formally expelled by his political party. Yet through sheer, unbending willpower, courageous constitutional independence, and masterly diplomacy, he preserved the executive office and expanded the republic by an empire. He proved to history that a president standing alone, armed only with conviction and the Constitution, could reshape the destiny of a continent forever.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The annexation of Texas reshaped the North American continent and set the stage for America to become a two-ocean superpower. John Tyler's tenacity ensured that the Lone Star Republic found its permanent home under the American flag. Next week, we turn to America's eleventh President, James K. Polk—the iron-willed workhorse of the presidency who promised to achieve four monumental goals, took on the British Empire over the Oregon boundary with the battle cry 'Fifty-Four Forty or Fight,' and fulfilled every promise in a single term. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
